factor-markets-s1.title: Tallow Candle Works: workers and output

table.caption: Daily output at Tallow Candle Works, which sells candles in a perfectly competitive market at \$2 each (invented data for practice)

factor-markets-s2.title: Welders at the Brackwater boatyards
factor-markets-s2.text: Brackwater is an invented harbor town where several boatyards build small fishing boats. Each boat needs many hours of welding. This year a new fish-processing plant opens nearby, and local fishing crews want more boats. The boatyards begin looking for more welders, and the welders' union reports that boatyards are offering more hours.

factor-markets-s3.title: Two firms add workers: a price taker and a single seller

table.caption: Firm X sells in a perfectly competitive market at \$10 a unit. Firm Y is the only seller of its good, so it must cut its price to sell more, and its marginal revenue is below its price. Both have the same marginal product (invented data for practice).
cols: Firm X: marginal revenue per unit
Firm Y: marginal revenue per unit

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal product of the third worker, in candles per day?

why.correct: Marginal product is the change in total product from one more worker: 75 - 55 = 20 candles.

mistakes.why: 25 is the average product of three workers (75 ÷ 3). Marginal product is the change in output from the third worker alone: 75 - 55.
75 is total product with three workers. The third worker adds only the change: 75 - 55 = 20.

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal revenue product of the fourth worker, in dollars per day?

why.correct: The fourth worker adds 90 - 75 = 15 candles, and for a competitive seller each candle adds the price, \$2, to revenue. MRP = MP × MR = 15 × \$2 = \$30.

mistakes.why: \$180 is the revenue from all four workers' output (90 × \$2). MRP uses the fourth worker's marginal product only: 15 × \$2.
15 is the marginal product in candles. Multiply by the marginal revenue of a candle, \$2, to get dollars.

items.q: In the table, why does each added worker bring in less revenue than the one before?
options: The price of candles falls as the firm hires more workers
Later workers are paid a lower wage than earlier ones
Each worker adds fewer candles at the same \$2 price
Total product falls after the second worker

why.correct: MRP = MP × MR. Here MR is the \$2 price for every candle, so MRP falls only because marginal product falls: 30, 25, 20, 15, 10 candles.
options: A perfectly competitive seller takes the market price; \$2 holds for every candle it sells.
The wage is a cost of a worker, not part of the revenue that worker brings in.
Right: marginal product falls (diminishing marginal returns) while the price stays at \$2, so MRP falls.
Total product keeps rising, to 100 candles; it rises by smaller amounts.

items.q: Use the table. The market price of candles rises from \$2 to \$3. What is the new marginal revenue product of the second worker, in dollars per day?

why.correct: The second worker still adds 55 - 30 = 25 candles. At \$3 each, MRP = 25 × \$3 = \$75, up from \$50.

mistakes.why: \$50 is the MRP at the old price. A higher product price raises every worker's MRP: use \$3.
\$165 uses total product with two workers. MRP uses the second worker's marginal product, 25 candles.

items.q: In the scenario, why do the boatyards want more welders?
options: Buyers want more boats, and welders' work is needed to build them
Welders have decided to work more hours this year
The boatyards earn revenue from selling welding services to crews
A welder is a good that households buy for their own use

why.correct: This is derived demand: firms want a factor because buyers want the product the factor helps produce.
options: Right: the demand for welders comes from the demand for the boats they help make.
That would be a change on the sellers' side of the market for welders, not the boatyards' reason for hiring.
The boatyards sell boats; welding is an input they buy.
Welders' work is a factor of production that firms buy, not a consumer good.

items.q: In the scenario, in which market do the boatyards buy welders' work, and who sells it?
options: A product market, where households sell finished boats to the boatyards
A product market, where firms sell labor to households
A factor market, where firms sell boats to fishing crews
A factor market, where households sell their labor to firms

why.correct: Factor markets are where labor, land and capital are bought and sold. Households (here, welders) sell; firms (the boatyards) buy.
options: Boats are sold by the boatyards (firms) in a product market; welding work is traded in a factor market.
Firms buy labor; they do not sell it to households.
Boats are a product, and they are traded in a product market.
Right: labor is a factor of production; households sell it and firms buy it.

items.q: In the scenario, which later event would most likely lead the boatyards to want fewer welders?
options: More fishing crews move to Brackwater
The fish-processing plant closes and crews order fewer boats
The price of a new fishing boat rises
Welders find new tools that let them weld faster

why.correct: The demand for a factor is derived from the demand for the product. Less demand for boats means a lower price for boats and a lower MRP for each welder.
options: More crews would raise the demand for boats and so for welders.
Right: lower demand for boats lowers the price of boats and the revenue each welder brings in, so the boatyards want fewer welders.
A higher boat price raises the revenue each welder's work brings in, so boatyards want more welders.
Faster welding raises each welder's marginal product, so each welder is worth more to a boatyard.

items.q: Use the table. What is Firm Y's marginal revenue product of the third worker, in dollars?

why.correct: MRP = MP × MR. The third worker adds 4 units, and each adds \$6 of marginal revenue for Firm Y: 4 × \$6 = \$24.

mistakes.why: \$40 multiplies by \$10, a price taker's marginal revenue. Firm Y must cut its price to sell more, so each extra unit adds only its own marginal revenue, \$6.
\$60 multiplies marginal revenue by price. MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue: 4 × \$6.

items.q: Use the table. What is Firm X's marginal revenue product of the second worker, in dollars?

why.correct: Firm X is a price taker, so its marginal revenue is the price, \$10. MRP = 5 × \$10 = \$50.

mistakes.why: \$40 uses Firm Y's marginal revenue. Firm X sells every unit at \$10, so its MR is \$10.
11 adds two marginal products. MRP is one worker's marginal product times marginal revenue: 5 × \$10.

items.q: Use the table. Why does Firm Y's MRP fall faster than Firm X's as each firm adds workers?
options: Firm Y's workers have a smaller marginal product than Firm X's
Firm Y's marginal revenue falls as well as its marginal product
Firm X can charge a higher price than Firm Y for each unit
Firm X's marginal revenue rises as it sells more units

why.correct: MRP = MP × MR. For a price taker MR is the constant price; for a single seller MR falls as output rises, because it lowers the price on every unit to sell one more.
options: The table gives both firms the same marginal product for each worker.
Right: both firms face falling MP, but only Firm Y also faces falling MR, so its MRP drops faster.
The table compares marginal revenue, not prices; the gap comes from Firm Y's marginal revenue falling as it sells more.
A price taker's marginal revenue stays at the price, \$10.

items.q: What is a factor market?
options: A market where households buy finished goods from firms
A market where a government sets the price of each input
A market where firms sell goods to other countries
A market where firms buy labor, land and capital from their owners

why.correct: In a factor market, households (and other owners of resources) sell labor, land and capital, and firms buy them. Payments are wages, rent and interest.
options: That is a product market.
Prices in factor markets are usually set by buyers and sellers; who sets them is not what defines the market.
Selling abroad is trade in goods, which happens in product markets.
Right: factor markets trade the inputs used to make goods and services.

items.q: Why is the demand for a factor of production called a derived demand?
options: Buyers want the product that the factor helps make
The factor's price is figured out by a formula set by the firm
Workers derive satisfaction from the goods they make
The factor's demand curve is drawn from the firm's total cost

why.correct: A bakery does not want bakers for their own sake; it wants them because people buy bread. If bread demand falls, the bakery wants fewer bakers.
options: Right: the factor's value to the firm comes from the product's value to buyers.
Derived refers to where the demand comes from, not to how a price is calculated.
Workers' satisfaction is about the sellers of labor; derived demand is about the buyers.
It comes from the revenue the factor brings in (its MRP), which depends on the product's demand.

items.q: A firm sells its output in a perfectly competitive market. Which expression gives the marginal revenue product of a worker?
options: Marginal revenue × price
Total product × price
Marginal product × price
Marginal product ÷ price

why.correct: MRP is the extra revenue from one more worker: the extra output (MP) times the extra revenue per unit (MR). In perfect competition MR = P.
options: This multiplies two dollar amounts per unit and leaves out the worker's output. MRP = MP × MR.
That is the revenue from all the workers' output, not from one more worker.
Right: for a price taker, marginal revenue equals price, so MRP = MP × MR = MP × P.
Dividing gives units of output per dollar, a different measure. MRP multiplies MP by the revenue each unit adds.

items.q: Why is a firm's MRP curve its demand curve for labor?
options: It shows how many people want to work at each wage
It shows the firm's total cost of hiring each number of workers
It shows how much output each worker makes on average
It shows what each added worker is worth to the firm

why.correct: At a given wage, the firm keeps hiring while a worker adds at least that much revenue. So the MRP schedule tells how many workers the firm wants at each wage: its demand for labor.
options: That describes the people offering to work, the sellers in the market, not the firm.
Costs are a different curve; MRP measures revenue added by each worker.
That is average product, not the extra revenue from one more worker.
Right: a firm is willing to pay up to a worker's MRP, so the MRP curve gives the quantity of labor it wants at each wage.

items.q: A new machine lets each of a firm's workers produce more output. The product price does not change. What happens to the MRP of each worker?
options: It falls, because the machine replaces some workers
It rises, because each worker's marginal product rises
It stays the same, because the price of the product is unchanged
It rises, because the price of the product rises

why.correct: Higher productivity raises marginal product at each quantity of labor, so MRP rises even with the same product price.
options: The question says each worker makes more; that raises MP and MRP at each quantity of labor.
Right: MRP = MP × MR, and MP is higher at every number of workers.
MRP depends on MP as well as the price; a rise in MP raises MRP.
The price is unchanged here; MRP rises through marginal product.

items.q: Hiring one more worker raises a firm's output by 8 units. Each extra unit adds \$5 to the firm's revenue. What is that worker's marginal revenue product, in dollars?

mistakes.why: 13 adds the two numbers. MRP multiplies the extra output by the extra revenue per unit: 8 × \$5.
1.6 divides. MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue.

items.q: Put the links in order: buyers start wanting more bicycles, and a bike maker hires more assemblers.
options: Demand for bicycles increases
The price of bicycles rises
Each assembler's MRP rises (MP × the higher price)
The bike maker wants to hire more assemblers at each wage

why.correct: Derived demand runs from the product to the factor: more demand for the product, a higher product price, a higher MRP for each worker, and so more workers wanted at each wage.

items.q: Which of these are payments made in a factor market? Select all that apply.
options: Wages a garage pays its mechanics
Rent a farmer pays for a field
The price a shopper pays for a loaf of bread
A shoe store's revenue from selling sneakers
A sales tax paid on a new phone

why.correct: Factor payments are wages (labor), rent (land), interest (capital) and profit (entrepreneurship).
options: Right: wages are the payment for labor.
Right: rent is the payment for land.
Bread is a finished good, bought in a product market.
Revenue from selling goods comes from a product market.
A tax on a purchase of a good is part of a product-market sale, not a factor payment.

items.q: Which of these is a transaction in a factor market?
options: A student buys a coffee at the café
A café sells gift cards to customers
A café hires a weekend barista
A family buys a used car from a neighbor

why.correct: In a factor market the firm is the buyer and the owner of labor, land or capital is the seller.
options: Coffee is a product sold to a household.
That is a sale of the café's product.
Right: the café is buying labor, a factor of production.
A car bought for the family's own use is a consumer good.

items.q: The price of a good falls, and nothing else changes. What happens to the marginal revenue product of the workers who make it?
options: It falls at every quantity of labor
It rises, because the good is cheaper to make
It stays the same, because marginal product is unchanged
It falls for the first worker and rises for the others

why.correct: For a competitive seller MRP = MP × P. A lower P lowers MRP for every worker.
options: Right: each worker makes the same output, but each unit now brings in less revenue.
A lower selling price lowers revenue per unit; it says nothing about cost.
MRP = MP × MR; with MR lower, MRP falls even though MP is the same.
The lower price lowers the revenue from every worker's output.
